extracted.intended_audience: legislators, political philosophers, legal reformers, and educated readers interested in law and government
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive principles for making and judging laws, punishments, and institutions across different forms of government (republic, aristocracy, monarchy, despotism), addressing torture, penalties, sumptuary laws, women's condition, and public mores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of torture (la question)
rubrics_metrics.description: «La question contre les criminels n'est pas dans un cas forcé... Elle n'est donc pas nécessaire par sa nature.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu argues that well-policed nations (example: England) reject torture without harm; ancient practices show many restrictions (Athens, Romans, Wisigoths). He concedes torture might suit despotic governments where fear is central, but the 'voice of nature' opposes it. Historical examples and legal limits (e.g., no preparatory question among Athenians, limited application among Romans) are cited as guidance against routine use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal presumptions favoring social trust
rubrics_metrics.description: «Parce que les hommes sont méchants, la loi est obligée de les supposer meilleurs qu'ils ne sont. Ainsi la déposition de deux témoins suffit... On juge aussi que tout enfant conçu pendant le mariage est légitime: la loi a confiance en la mère...»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The law should rely on simple presumptions (two witnesses, legitimacy of children conceived in marriage) to facilitate administration of justice and social order. These presumptions are pragmatic devices to operate the legal system despite human vice; they are not absolute but serve as default rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and moderation between pecuniary and corporal punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: «Un bon législateur prend un juste milieu: il n'ordonne pas toujours des peines pécuniaires; il n'inflige pas toujours des peines corporelles.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators should balance fines and corporal penalties, considering social values: Germans preferred pecuniary penalties, Japanese rejected them; fines can be scaled to fortune, and infamy can be joined to monetary penalties. Avoid one-size-fits-all punishment systems; tailor to social context and wealth distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temper and limit the law of talion
rubrics_metrics.description: «Les États despotiques... usent beaucoup de la loi du talion; les États modérés la reçoivent quelquefois: mais... les premiers la font exercer rigoureusement, et que les autres lui donnent presque toujours des tempéraments.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While harsh retaliation (talion) may be common in despotic states, moderate states should temper it—permit conversion of corporal penalties into damages, as in the Twelve Tables and Wisigothic laws. Use monetary compensation or other mitigations rather than strict equal bodily retaliation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid punishing parents for children's crimes
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of systems (e.g., China, ancient Peru) that punish fathers for children's faults as 'despotic' practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Montesquieu rejects collective family punishments as indicative of despotism. Social shame or honor among relatives may substitute, but formal legal punishment of parents for children's crimes is improper except where cultural context makes it meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clemency appropriate to monarchy but must be prudent
rubrics_metrics.description: «La clémence est la qualité distinctive des monarques... On la distingue aisément de cette faiblesse qui mène le prince au mépris et à l'impuissance même de punir.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clemency secures affection and glory for monarchs and often substitutes for harsh penalties where disgrace suffices. However, rulers must balance clemency against the need for authority—avoid indulgence that undermines capacity to punish. Historical examples (emperors Maurice, Anastasius, Isaac) illustrate extremes and dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Luxury rises with inequality and urban concentration
rubrics_metrics.description: «Le luxe est toujours en proportion avec l'inégalité des fortunes... Le luxe est encore en proportion avec la grandeur des villes, et surtout de la capitale...»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawmakers should view luxury as a function of wealth inequality, national riches, and urban aggregation. Policies addressing luxury must consider these structural causes; simply outlawing luxury without addressing inequality or urbanization is ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sumptuary laws in republics should maintain equality and proceed cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: «Dans les républiques... moins il y a de luxe dans une république, plus elle est parfaite... Les lois du nouveau partage des champs... étaient salutaires par leur nature. Elles ne sont dangereuses que comme action subite.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In republics, sumptuary laws can preserve civic virtue and equality, but redistributive measures must be gradual to avoid family and societal upheaval. Rapid, radical changes to wealth distribution risk general instability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibit aristocratic luxury to preserve moderation
rubrics_metrics.description: «L'aristocratie mal constituée a ce malheur que les nobles y ont les richesses, et que cependant ils ne doivent pas dépenser; le luxe... en doit être banni.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In aristocracies where nobles hoard wealth, laws should enforce modesty and redirect elite expenditures to public or civic uses (festivities, public offices). Venice's legal enforcement of noble modesty is offered as an example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow and manage luxury in monarchies for economic sustainability
rubrics_metrics.description: «Comme, par la constitution des monarchies, les richesses se sont inégalement partagées, il faut bien qu'il y ait du luxe... Il faut même que les riches y dépensent à proportion de l'inégalité des fortunes...»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In monarchies, luxury plays an economic role: wealthy spending circulates goods and maintains livelihoods. Lawmakers should avoid imposing sumptuary laws that stifle this mechanism; instead, allow luxury to scale with inequality to sustain the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use sumptuary laws only for absolute frugality or protection of domestic industry
rubrics_metrics.description: «Les lois somptuaires peuvent avoir aussi pour objet une frugalité relative... et c'est l'esprit des lois que l'on a faites de nos jours en Suède.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sumptuary laws are appropriate when aimed at strict frugality (e.g., Aragon's 13th-century food restrictions) or to prevent harmful imports and protect domestic production (Sweden's bans on exquisite wines, precious wares). Their suitability depends on the state's wealth and economic needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate luxury according to population-resource balance
rubrics_metrics.description: «Pour savoir s'il faut encourager le luxe ou le proscrire, on doit d'abord jeter les yeux sur le rapport qu'il y a entre le nombre du peuple et la facilité de le faire vivre.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where soil and production barely feed the population (example: China), luxury is pernicious and laws must enforce frugality and direct labor to necessary arts; where production exceeds subsistence (England, France), luxury is less dangerous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curbe luxury to preserve regime longevity
rubrics_metrics.description: Argument from Chinese history: repeated dynastic revolutions result from luxury, corruption, and subsequent weakening of ruling families.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Excessive luxury leads to regime decay—decline of virtue among rulers, rise of parasitic court classes, weakened succession—so long-term stability requires restraining luxury, especially in large agrarian empires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminalize and proscribe public sexual incontinence in republics
rubrics_metrics.description: «...on peut regarder dans un État populaire l'incontinence publique comme le dernier des malheurs... les bons législateurs y ont-ils exigé des femmes une certaine gravité de moeurs. Ils ont proscrit... non seulement le vice, mais l'apparence même du vice.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public sexual immorality corrupts civic virtue; republics should legislate not only against vice but against its appearance, excluding practices that produce idleness and moral corruption. Enforcement may target public behaviors and institutions that encourage gallantry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tailor laws about women to the nature of the government
rubrics_metrics.description: «Les femmes ont peu de retenue dans les monarchies... Dans les États despotiques, les femmes n'introduisent point le luxe, mais elles sont elles-mêmes un objet de luxe... Dans les républiques, les femmes sont libres par les lois, et captivées par les moeurs...»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators should adapt rules governing women to the regime: monarchies tend to produce courtly freedom and vanity; despotisms treat women as objects of luxury and require strict seclusion; republics rely on social mores rather than legal coercion. Policy must reflect these regime-specific dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domestic/matrimonial tribunals function only when supported by social mores
rubrics_metrics.description: On the Roman 'tribunal domestique': it judged women's conduct and supplemented civic magistrates; such tribunals presuppose existing mores and deliver arbitrary, non-codified penalties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions that police private morality (e.g., domestic tribunals) work only where shared customs exist; moral infractions are hard to codify, and such tribunals inevitably exercise discretionary/arbitrary penalties. Use them cautiously and only where mores justify them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt institutions to changing mores; avoid obsolete public accusation mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: «L'accusation publique... fit que ces deux choses tombèrent avec les moeurs, et finirent avec la république.»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal mechanisms (public accusations, domestic tribunals) should be revised as social mores and governmental forms evolve. What worked in a republic (public accusation) may be inappropriate in a monarchy and may be abolished as mores change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against political abuse of moral laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of Roman emperors using laws against female debauchery (e.g., law Julia) as instruments of tyranny and vengeance rather than moral reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral legislation can be perverted to target political rivals; legislators should ensure penalties align with the law's original, limited intent and avoid empowering rulers to weaponize morality for political ends. Historical examples: Augustus and Tiberius manipulating laws to punish relatives and elites.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate dowries according to regime needs
rubrics_metrics.description: «Les dots doivent être considérables dans les monarchies... Elles doivent être médiocres dans les républiques...»
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dowry regulation should reflect regime structure: large dowries in monarchies help husbands sustain rank and the luxury expected of court life; modest dowries in republics limit luxury and support equality. Use dowry policy as a tool to align family economics with political order.
